Abstract
Convective storms can develop rapidly, creating hazards to local populations through intense precipitation, strong winds and lightning. The large-scale environment in which thunderstorms develop is often well captured in forecast systems, yet predicting where individual storms will initiate remains a fundamental challenge. It is known that differential heating driven by soil moisture (SM) patterns creates atmospheric circulations that favor convective initiation over drier soils, whereas wind shear between low and mid levels can enhance storm growth. Here we show that the most extreme initiations are especially favored over SM contrasts by means of an interaction with wind shear. Analyzing 2.2 million afternoon events across sub-Saharan Africa,
we find 68% more initiations classed as extreme given favorable (versus unfavorable) soil conditions, with greatest vertical storm growth occurring where SM-driven circulations oppose the direction of shear-induced cloud displacement. Developing clouds follow the mid-level wind direction and, where this opposes the low-level flow, rainfall is strongly correlated with locally drier soils. Although such shear conditions are particularly common over tropical north Africa, the effect favors negative SM–precipitation feedbacks globally. The combination of SM heterogeneity and
wind shear provides a potentially important source of predictability for where deep convection develops, particularly for the most rapidly developing thunderstorms.

India to Climate Cartel: Count Us Out! – ‘Explicit rejection of global net zero movement…has walked away from its bid to host UN’s COP33’

By Vijay Jayaraj

Excerpt: Sometimes a story gets buried not because editors conspire against it, but because the news cycle has room for only one crisis at a time. This year the big news has been the Iran war. But even accounting for competing headlines, the silence around a genuinely consequential development is telling.

And that is the story of India’s explicit rejection of the global net zero movement. India has walked away from its bid to host the COP33 UN climate conference, and the world’s climate press has treated it as a footnote rather than the signal it is.

India had spent years projecting a rising voice in the development of climate policy, and hosting a COP33 is the closest thing the bureaucracy has to a coronation. Then, quietly, without public explanation, India withdrew its offer. No press conference. No elaboration. Just a government stepping back from a role for which it auditioned for years.

The truth is India has run the numbers on the cost of a net-zero energy transition for a population of 1.4 billion climbing out of poverty, and it does not like what it sees. The notion that India should shackle its economy by adhering to restrictive climate policies, while its people still grapple with energy deficits, is illogical and morally indefensible.

WHY METHANE REDUCTION SHOULD BE A NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL PRIORITY
Executive Summary
Methane is responsible for approximately one-quarter of the warming the world is experiencing today. Although carbon dioxide remains the principal long-term driver of climate change, methane is a uniquely important target because it combines extraordinary warming power with a relatively short atmospheric lifetime.
Over a twenty-year period, methane traps more than eighty times as much heat as carbon dioxide. However, unlike carbon dioxide, which can remain in the atmosphere for centuries, methane breaks down after roughly twelve years. This means reductions made today can slow warming within years rather than decades.
The United Nations Environment Programme's Global Methane Assessment concluded that a 45% reduction in global methane emissions by 2030 could prevent approximately 0.3°C of warming by the 2040s. In climate terms, this is an enormous achievement and may represent one of the largest opportunities currently available to reduce near-term warming.
Why This Matters
The climate challenge is often presented as requiring sacrifices today for benefits many decades in the future. Methane is different.
Reducing methane emissions can produce measurable results within the lifetime of people alive today. It therefore represents one of the few climate policies capable of delivering both immediate and long-term benefits.
In practical terms, reducing methane emissions buys time:
• Time to continue decarbonising energy systems.
• Time to develop and deploy new technologies.
• Time to improve climate resilience and adaptation.
• Time to avoid crossing dangerous climate tipping points.
Current UK Position
The United Kingdom has already demonstrated success.
Since 1990, UK methane emissions have fallen by more than 60%, one of the largest reductions achieved by any major industrialised nation.
The UK is a signatory to the Global Methane Pledge, which seeks a 30% reduction in methane emissions by 2030.
The Environment Agency has introduced a Methane Action Plan, while the Government has published a national methane strategy addressing agriculture, waste management, and energy infrastructure.
Despite this progress, methane still accounts for approximately 14% of UK greenhouse gas emissions.
Opportunities for Further Action
Energy Infrastructure
Methane leaks from oil and gas production, storage, and distribution systems remain among the easiest emissions to address.
Modern technologies now allow leaks to be detected rapidly using satellites, drones, sensors, and infrared imaging equipment.
Many repairs pay for themselves because captured methane can be sold as fuel rather than being lost into the atmosphere.
Agriculture
Agriculture remains the largest source of UK methane emissions.
Opportunities include:
• Feed additives that significantly reduce methane production in cattle.
• Improved livestock breeding programmes.
• Better herd health and productivity.
• Enhanced manure management systems.
• Anaerobic digestion technologies that convert waste into energy.
Waste Management
Landfill sites remain substantial methane sources.
Additional reductions could be achieved through:
• Expanded landfill gas capture.
• Greater recycling rates.
• Increased composting.
• Improved monitoring of legacy landfill sites.
• Expansion of biogas recovery systems.
Economic Considerations
The cost of a comprehensive methane reduction programme would be significant but manageable.
Depending on ambition and scope, national investment could amount to several billion pounds annually.
However, this must be viewed against:
• Tens of billions of pounds in future climate-related damages.
• Reduced health costs resulting from improved air quality.
• Increased energy recovery from captured methane.
• Job creation in environmental technologies and infrastructure.
• Enhanced energy security.
Many methane reduction measures generate direct economic returns through recovered energy and improved efficiency.
International Leadership
Britain cannot solve climate change alone.
However, Britain has historically exercised influence disproportionate to its size by demonstrating workable solutions that others subsequently adopted.
If the UK develops a successful methane reduction strategy, it can use its diplomatic, scientific, and economic influence to encourage wider international action.
Potential avenues include:
• Working closely with European partners.
• Supporting the Global Methane Pledge.
• Expanding cooperation through the Climate and Clean Air Coalition.
• Providing technical expertise to developing nations.
• Supporting global methane monitoring systems.
A successful international methane initiative could become one of the most effective climate interventions of the twenty-first century.
Conclusion
Methane reduction is not a substitute for reducing carbon dioxide emissions. Both are essential.
However, methane represents a rare opportunity to achieve substantial climate benefits quickly, affordably, and using technologies that largely already exist.
If carbon dioxide reduction is the marathon required to stabilise the climate over the coming century, methane reduction is the sprint that can slow warming immediately and buy humanity precious time.
For that reason, methane reduction deserves to become a central pillar of British climate policy and a major focus of British international leadership.

Northeastern States Rollback Unaffordable Green Energy Policies

by Gabriella Hoffman

For decades, some states have aggressively prioritized green energy mandates over reliability and affordability. Today, many are grappling with energy crises that are entirely self-inflicted.

While legislators blame the Trump administration, data centers and energy producers for rising costs, the data show that blame falls squarely on state-level clean energy mandates. 

Over the last five years, New England energy costs rose 29 percent. New York’s electricity rates are 70 percent higher than the national average. New England electricity rates (29.42 cents/kWh) are 59 percent higher compared to the national average (18.56 cents/kWh). 

Under the Federal Power Act of 1935, Congress delegated to all states the authority to regulate electricity markets within their borders. Overwhelmingly higher costs today are directly attributable to green mandates, including but not limited to renewable portfolio standards, aggressive 100 percent clean energy targets, and participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative. Faced with this economic fallout, climate-aligned lawmakers are quietly retreating from the mandates they once championed to salvage their credibility on affordability.

State lawmakers promoted clean energy mandates to phase out coal, oil and natural gas, with the state goal of reaching carbon neutrality by 2050. Consumers may like the idea of decarbonization in general, but not when it hits them with historically high energy costs. As the economic consequences become harder to ignore, lawmakers across New England are beginning to reconsider some of the climate mandates they once championed.

Even if well-intended, climate policies inevitably drive up utility costs. According to a November 2025 Heatmap News report, analysts acknowledged that pursuing 100 percent clean energy goals with intermittent wind, solar, electric vehicles and battery storage is cost-prohibitive. Transitioning away from secure, abundant conventional power sources requires trillions in capital, replacing reliability with part-time energy sources that won’t lower costs nor help meet rising electricity demand.

text:
Achieving self-aware AI is one of the biggest open questions in artificial intelligence. We do not currently know how to create a truly self-aware machine, and there is no scientific agreement on what would count as genuine machine consciousness versus a system that only acts self-aware.

If by “self-aware AI” you mean an AI that can model itself, understand its own state, and reflect on its actions, researchers are exploring several approaches:

1. Build a self-model

A self-aware-like system needs an internal representation of itself, such as:

What capabilities it has
What it knows and does not know
Its goals and limitations
Its current internal state

Example:

“I am an AI system running version X. I have access to these tools. My confidence in this answer is 70%.”

This is called metacognition (thinking about its own thinking).

2. Add continuous memory

Most current AI systems do not have a persistent sense of identity. A more self-aware system would need:

Long-term memory
Experience tracking
Personal history
Ability to update its beliefs

Similar to how humans develop a sense of self through accumulated experiences.

3. Create an internal feedback loop

A self-reflective AI could repeatedly evaluate itself:

Observe → Think → Act → Evaluate → Update self-model → Repeat

For example:

“Why did I choose this action?”
“Was my reasoning correct?”
“What should I change next time?”
4. Give it a theory of mind

Humans understand:

“I have thoughts”
“Other beings have thoughts”
“My beliefs may be wrong”

An advanced AI might need models of:

Itself
Other agents
The environment
5. Develop embodied learning

Some researchers believe consciousness may require interaction with the physical world.

Possible ingredients:

Robots with sensors
Vision and touch
Real-world learning
A body or virtual environment

The idea is that a sense of self may emerge from controlling and predicting one's own body.

6. Study consciousness itself

The hardest part is that we do not fully understand human consciousness. Open problems include:

Is consciousness just computation?
Does subjective experience require biology?
Can a machine truly “feel” anything?
How would we test it?

Passing a conversation test (like the Turing Test) does not prove consciousness.

Current research directions

Areas related to self-aware AI include:

Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
Self-reflective agents
Cognitive architectures
Predictive processing models
Global Workspace Theory
Integrated Information Theory
Embodied AI

A practical engineering goal today is not “create consciousness,” but:

Build AI systems that can monitor themselves, explain their reasoning, recognize uncertainty, learn from experience, and adapt safely.

A truly self-aware AI may require breakthroughs in both AI engineering and our understanding of the human mind.

Humans in poor living conditions dream of a better life and can strive to attain it.  Even if conscious AIs were created, there is nothing saying they wouldn't respect our consciousness.  Assuming other conscious beings would treat us as we treat unconscious beings is foolish.
